doc.title: Hal Espinosa interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, March 20, 2024

title: No career plans: sports, Arizona State scholarship and first pro jobs
summary: Hal never saw trumpet as a career; he won a scholarship to Arizona State and played jobs at 17 with Nat King Cole and Ted Lewis around Phoenix.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: So going back to this list, if you’re thinking about eventually a career as a trumpet player, I was just interested in a few of the songs off this list from 1950 and we have the “Tennessee Waltz” by Patti Page, “Cry of the Wild Goose” by Frankie Laine, and the “Third Man Theme” by the fellow who used to play on New Year’s Eve, remember Guy Lombardo?
I guess my point is the big band era had faded out for the most part. What were your aspirations and how did you see that playing a trumpet could be a career?

Well you know at that time I never thought of playing the trumpet as a career. It was just a fun thing to do and it became more fun as I got better naturally, and then finally I got to be on first chair in high school. And I was really into sports except I’m not tall and I’m not big heavy wise, and I loved baseball, basketball, football and I was good at it in junior

high school but when I got to high school all these kids that were my size or a couple of inches taller just grew like a foot taller. So finally I, you know the fact that I was practicing a lot a couple of guys from the high school band went to Arizona State on scholarships, and they’d come back and tell me, “Harold, you’ve got to audition for a scholarship.” So I thought why not, I’ll do that. So two of us went over and I got a scholarship. So at that time I got free tuition plus $100 for the year. You know to buy books and things like that. And my dad worked for the railroad so I got free transportation over to Tempe, Arizona from Riverside at that time, so there was no cost there. So I really didn’t plan on playing professionally, I just wanted to go to college. Went to college but then in the band I was able — they saw me as a hot shot trumpet player from California. I was no hot shot but I can hold my own fairly well. So then some guys in Phoenix heard about me and had me play professionally with them. I was 17 and Nat King Cole came into town and there’s one restaurant — not restaurant, but a, oh what would I call it — a regular club where there’s entertainment. And Nat King Cole came in, I worked for him for a week at 17 and I thought wow, you know, everything — love this. And then pretty soon Ted — what’s his last name, he always had the top hat?
Oh yeah, I know who you mean.

He goes way back. But I think he fooled around with the clarinet. And it’s been so long ago I don’t remember now. But anyway I worked for him. And then a movie came into town and I got to do some sidelining on a movie and I thought you know this is really a great way to make money. And I was making money then as a kid playing in these jobs. And I’d do a few casuals while I was in college. So only then did I start thinking I wonder if I could ever be good enough to play professionally. Because in high school I’d hear Les Brown playing “Leap Frog” and I’d try to do it and [scats] crack-crack. And pretty soon I got it down pretty good.
